It was not the surveyor who made a mistake.
What stopped the ship was an amendment.
The classification society to which the owner sent the surveys worked for one state only.
The state whose flag she flies had not ratified the protocol.
A convention does not become law on the day it is adopted.
It was not the surveyor who made a mistake, and it was not the master.
What stopped the ship was an amendment that one state had accepted.
Liability did not follow the fault; it followed the flag.

Three different lawyers asked me the same question, and my answer is always the same. I surveyed that ship under the rules her flag state had accepted. Those are the only rules I am allowed to use. My authorisation comes from one state only. The port on the other side of the ocean had ratified a protocol that her flag state had not. That is not a mistake in my survey, and I cannot change it. The hard part for people is this: both certificates were valid. Mine was valid under the law of the flag. Theirs was valid under the law of the port. And in the port, the law of the port always wins.
